en: Has surely taken his child with him.
The White Holy Elder to whom he pledged his hand,
Saying, “He is left from my Manas,”
Has surely reached his orphan Semetey.
Enticing your child,
They have surely taken him with them.
Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
When a falcon flies from the nest,
A hawk remains in its place.
My foal, was Manas not my falcon?
Is my child not my hawk?
When a white hawk flies from the nest,
Its female goshawk remains upon the perch.
When my white hawk leaves this world,
Its child remains in its place.
My white hawk Manas, my foal,
Was no khan to depart without offspring.
King Manas, my foal,
Was no man to remain childless.
Do not grieve and weep, my child!
Oh, my foal Kanykey,
Do not torment your mourning soul!
The spring flowing from the hills,
Our God will show us
The only child, Semetey!
Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
He was a lion favored by the unseen patron.
The Forty Hidden Saints, the unseen ones and Kyzyr
Accompanied that warrior.
They have surely taken him with them.
Through Üyrülmö’s three marshes,
Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
Search three days before despairing.
Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
Run to and fro.
When my hero Manas was alive,
In his cradle days,
On some days, as he lay,
Poised like a darting snake,
He would sometimes go away;
My Manas vanished just like this.
On some days my Manas,
While in his cradle,
Became unseen and disappeared.
He is a lion who takes after his father.
Some of his protectors
Have now stirred my child to movement.
Along the ravine, unable to keep still,
Perhaps he has gone away to play.
Vanishing from sight,
Perhaps my child has crawled away.
The grassy plain covered with fescue,
Kanykey, search carefully through it!”
As the old woman spoke in agitation,
Your dear mother Chyyyrdy,
When she said these words,
The fescue among plane trees and willows
She thoroughly searched.
Among dark sedge and white oatlike mountain grass,
She now looked for his tracks.
There was not a crow to caw.
As she searched and watched for his tracks,
There was not a raven to croak.
Wishing to die, unable to die,
Your mother wept in sobs,
Unable to give up her poor life,
Unable to find the child she sought.
As your sister-in-law went walking,
Unable to give up her poor life,
As your sister-in-law hurried on,
The one path he had followed—
The bend of the safe road.
Unable to find her orphan,
Your sister-in-law wandered in misery—
Such was the meagerness of her fortune.
“A place of calamity, this great poplar:
Why did I come and lodge here?” she said.
“Parted from my beloved,
What shall I do, O God?
I have become like an extinguished fire!” she said.
Grieving and sorrowing,
Her only one, whom she took as support—
How did she not die? Life was sweet.
Parted from Semetey,
It was night, not daytime.
Parted from her orphan,
It was a day of utter horror.
The rolling gray foothills
Your sister-in-law searched by reckoning.
No sign of him appeared there.
Your mother wept and screamed,
Then turned back again.
The spring at Oyurmaluu
She searched ten times.
Unable to find him in Oyurma,
Your formidable mother Kanykey
Clapped her palms together.
“Magnanimous Manas, would that you had not died!” she said,
And struck her dear head.
Screaming and weeping in anguish,
Unable to bear her burning grief,
Her dear, long thick hair
She tore out and flung away.
Then your mother Kanykey,
Her butterfly soul, through many places,
Kanykey drove in torment.
For the only one left by the fierce hero,
Kanykey searched.
Her dear, long thick hair,
Your mother went braiding.
“My lamp obtained at death’s door,” she said.
Your mother was near to death.
Her strength gone, she lamented and wept.
Her dear eyes, like blackcurrants,
Bled whenever she blinked.
“Bereft while fleeing,
There is no one unfortunate as I,” she said.
Then your mother’s strength departed.
The offspring left by the great steed—
Am I truly to be parted
From the lamp left by the white hawk?
When she came to the plane tree,
Unable indeed to find the orphan,
Kanykey stood wasting away.
Then, crying out, “My lamp!”
Kanykey stood howling.
“Parted from this fortune of mine,
O God, what wish can I attain?
My soft little mottled gray hawk,
My gray goshawk, my morning star!
Let me die right now!
The one I kissed with open mouth,
The one I saw when I opened my eyes,
Rather than this, I myself
Would die instead of remaining alive!
My spring flowing through the valley,
How can I remain without dying,
My lamp obtained at death’s door?
Affliction has fallen upon a fortunate head;
A night without dawn has fallen!
Parted from my only one,
Was this the day to suffer so?”
Your heroic mother Kanykey,
Suffering hardship and aching,
Her ribs, her limbs, her eighty bones,
Every one crumbling,
Unable to regain her composure,
Your mother screamed in helplessness.
Your tiger mother Chyyyrdy,
The old woman lay sleeping.
Utterly unconcerned,
That her orphan had disappeared,
(Your mother did not grieve.)
She did not give it the slightest regard.
Then your lion mother Chyyyrdy,
Pillowed upon the holy Quran,
Had fallen into unrestrained sleep.
Your mother lay with her head toward the qibla.
Kanykey grieved:
“Has my dear old mother
Reached the time of failing strength?
Or has my renowned, heroic mother
Reached the time to leave for Mecca?
Though I have lost her only one,
My mother does not grieve.
Or has her appointed death arrived?
His half-open eyes wandered wildly.
Is she ready to depart for Judgment?
With all her reason lost,
Has my beloved mother
Reached the time when she no longer knows?
Setting off toward Bukhara,
Has this storming, fierce woman
Reached her appointed death?
Without tormenting my soul so much,
My beloved, one God,
Make your decree more swiftly.
Azrael, taker of souls,
Stretch your five fingers toward me.
Let me enter the dug grave;
‘She was a renowned beauty,’ say,
And draw me in, black earth.
Parted from my orphan,
O God, how can I remain alive?
Rather than this, I, unfortunate,
Let me give up this accursed life.
Here on this slope I am left all alone;
How can I remain alive?
I was a moon: let me set behind the mountain.
My magnanimous lord, take me with you;
Let me lie foot to foot with you!
I was a sun: let me set in the ravine.
I have parted from my beloved.
With the magnanimous one gone to the afterlife,
Let me lie foot to foot.
My dear hair like a halter rope,
Why did I fail to braid it?
While my lord favored by Kyzyr was alive,
Why did I fail to die?
O God, fleeting world,
I said I would die from shame.
That I remain alive without dying—
Was he not left behind by him?—
Is for the suffering only child.
My dear eyes like a wild ram’s,
Is it time for them to burst apart?
From the only one left by the magnanimous one,
Parted here along the way,
Is this my time to be left crying, ‘Alas’?
O God, rubbing the flesh of my calves raw,
For whom did I set off walking?
Saying, ‘He was left behind by my khan,’
I came on alive without dying,
For the one child, Semetey!
Have my feet broken from walking?
Parted from my only one,
O God, has my soul found rest now?”
For six calves and four yearling horses,
Making a special dedication,
She had bought Ak Tinte, the Bright Dagger.
Drawing it from its sheath and clasping it,
To depart for Judgment,
Your mother set it against her slanting lower ribs,
To plunge the dagger into her lung,
Valuing her wretched life less than a hair,
Your mother was about to die.
She stood weeping with deep sobs.
Then dawn broke bright and clear;
Light fell upon the earth.
There in the hollow, from the dark cliff,
Semetey, left by Manas,
Born surpassing all within his nest—
His protector was Kozhosan.
It was the time he upheld the child.
The one who gave his hand was Ak Eshen,
Was leading him by the hand.
Kozhosan of the seven holy ones,
Drawing the child out of his cradle,
Had taken him away.
Enjoying the dark hollow,
He had gone away to play.
Down from the steep bank, Semetey
Had gone crawling.
Where his two hands had touched,
Hollows like hearths were scooped out.
Where his two knees had touched,
For the child blessed by Kozhosan,
Channels like irrigation ditches were gouged.
Then, following his trail, crying out,
Beseeching, 'O God!'
Your mother's tears poured forth.
Unable to wipe away her tears,
Your mother Kanykei,
Unable to check her running nose,
When she saw the trail he had taken,
Tears streamed from her eyes.
